title: LFM3 brings multimodal models to the edge
excerpt: LFM3 delivers 2 B-parameter text, vision, audio, omni and decision models that run on any device.
body:
A new family of 2 B-parameter models entered the open-weight arena this week. The LFM3 series bundles text, vision, audio, omni and decision capabilities onto a single backbone, and the first release already shows measurable gains over the previous generation.

The headline claim is that LFM3-1.7B matches the short-prompt performance of LFM2-1.2B while running about 25 % faster on an 8 K-token context. The post explains why that matters, how the architecture makes it possible, and what the practical workflow looks like for developers who want to specialize the models.

## More capability per parameter with a tri-hybrid backbone  

LFM3 replaces the pure short-convolution plus attention mix of LFM2 with a three-operator layer design. Of the 24 layers, 13 are gated short convolutions, five are sliding-window attention (SWA) blocks with a 256-token window, and six are global-attention blocks. The convolution kernel grew from size 3 to size 7, expanding the receptive field without a proportional speed hit.

The SWA blocks were chosen after an automated hardware-in-the-loop search because they give the best quality-speed trade-off for long contexts. The result is a model that retains the fast, on-device character of the earlier hybrid while delivering more expressive power per parameter. In practice, LFM3-1.7B reaches the same short-prompt accuracy as LFM2-1.2B despite using 35 % fewer parameters, and it processes an 8 K-token sequence about a quarter faster.

Additional tricks, head-wise gated attention, partial RoPE in global layers, and sandwich norm, help keep activations stable during quantization, which is essential for edge deployment.

## Designed for on-device inference across many hardware combos  

LFM3 was tested on 14 different device and backend pairings, ranging from high-end phones (Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, OnePlus 15) to a Raspberry Pi 5, Apple M4 Max, AMD Ryzen AI laptops, and various Arm and x86 cloud CPUs. The text model fits in about 1 GB when stored at 4-bit precision, a size that comfortably sits on most modern smartphones and embedded boards.

The expanded hardware-in-the-loop search that produced the tri-hybrid layer mix also verified that the added SWA and global-attention blocks do not erode the low-latency profile on these platforms. In other words, the same binary can run on a phone GPU, a laptop CPU, or a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU without needing separate model variants.

## Fine-tuning on a single GPU makes specialization easy  

All LFM3 variants are open-weight and available on Hugging Face, the Liquid AI Playground, and via the API ([source](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm3)). Because the base model sits at 1.7 B parameters, a single consumer-grade GPU can fine-tune the model on a custom dataset in a few hours.

The training recipe includes a mid-stage of 3.5 T high-quality tokens that emphasize agentic traces and tool-call patterns, extending the context window to 256 K tokens. This extra exposure means that after fine-tuning, the model retains the ability to handle long-form inputs while still fitting the target task.

A typical fine-tuning workflow looks like this:

1. Pull the base checkpoint from Hugging Face.  
2. Run the provided fine-tuning script with your dataset and the default hyper-parameters.  
3. Export the resulting model and apply the 4-bit quantization pipeline for on-device inference.

The steps require only a single GPU and a few hours of compute, after which the model can be deployed to any of the supported edge devices.

## New vision and audio encoders raise the multimodal ceiling  

Beyond the text model, LFM3 introduces flagship in-house vision and audio encoders that share the same 2 B-parameter backbone. Because the encoders inherit the tri-hybrid layer mix, they enjoy the same speed-per-parameter advantage as the text model.

Early benchmarks on the Liquid AI Playground show that the vision encoder can process a standard image on a mid-range phone GPU in well under a few hundred milliseconds, while the audio encoder handles a short clip in a comparable time frame on the same hardware. Those results illustrate that the multimodal family can serve real-time applications such as on-device OCR, speech-to-text, or visual question answering without offloading to a server.

## The takeaway  

LFM3 packs more expressive power per parameter by mixing gated convolutions, sliding-window attention and global attention in a tri-hybrid backbone. That design keeps inference fast on a wide range of edge hardware while still delivering a 25 % speed boost for 8 K-token contexts. Because the entire family is open-weight and fine-tunable on a single GPU, developers can quickly specialize a 2 B-parameter multimodal model and deploy it wherever their application runs.
